cues.text: How many equal square tiles would cover a small floor? A long piece of string cannot cover the surface. We need a different measure from perimeter: area tells us how much flat space a shape covers.
cues.asr_text: HOW MANY EQUAL SQUARE TILES WOULD COVER A SMALL FLOOR A LONG PIECE OF STRING CANNOT COVER THE SURFACE WE NEED A DIFFERENT MEASURE FROM PRIMETER AREA TELLS US HOW MUCH FLAT SPACE A SHAPE COVERS

cues.text: Our learning goal is to explain and find area using square units.
board: Explain and find area using square units.

board_events.text: Explain and find area using square units.

cues.text: Success criteria. I can cover a surface without gaps or overlaps. I can use rows and columns to count squares. I can distinguish area from perimeter.
board: 1. Cover a surface without gaps or overlaps.
2. Use rows and columns to count squares.
cues.asr_text: SUCCESS CRITERIA I CAN COVER A SURFACE WITHOUT GAPS OR OVERLAPS I CAN USE ROWS AND COLUMNS TO COUNT SQUARES I CAN DISTINGUISH AREA FROM PRIMETTA

board_events.text: 1. Cover a surface without gaps or overlaps.
2. Use rows and columns to count squares.

cues.text: Arrange equal unit squares without gaps or overlaps. Each square covers one square unit. For a rectangle, equal rows let us count efficiently with multiplication. A square centimetre is a square one centimetre along each side, not a one-centimetre length.
cues.asr_text: ARRANGE EQUAL UNIT SQUARES WITHOUT GAPS OR OVERLAPS EACH SQUARE COVERS ONE SQUARE UNIT FOR A RECTANGLE EQUAL ROWS LET US COUNT EFFICIENTLY WITH MULTIPLICATION A SQUARE CENTIMETER IS A SQUARE ONE CENTIMETER ALONG EACH SIDE NOT A ONE CENTIMETER LENGTH

cues.text: A rectangle has eight columns and five rows of square-centimetre tiles. Predict how many unit squares cover it. Each row contains eight squares, and there are five equal rows.
cues.asr_text: A RECTANGLE HAS EIGHT COLUMNS AND FIVE ROWS OF SQUARE CENTIMETER TILES PREDICT HOW MANY UNIT SQUARES COVER IT EACH ROW CONTAINS EIGHT SQUARES AND THERE ARE FIVE EQUAL ROWS

cues.text: Five groups of eight make forty unit squares. The area is forty square centimetres. Multiplying eight centimetres by five centimetres counts the same tiled surface, so we write the squared unit.
cues.asr_text: FIVE GROUPS OF EIGHT MAKE FORTY UNIT SQUARES THE AREA IS FORTY SQUARE CENTIMETERS MULTIPLYING EIGHT CENTIMETERS BY FIVE CENTIMETERS COUNTS THE SAME TILED SURFACE SO WE WRITE THE SQUARED UNIT

cues.text: A play mat is seven metres by four metres. Imagine covering it with one-metre squares. There are seven squares along each row, with four rows altogether. What would the surface measurement be?
cues.asr_text: A PLAYMART IS SEVEN METERS BY FOUR METRES IMAGINE COVERING IT WITH ONE METRE SQUARES THERE ARE SEVEN SQUARES ALONG EACH ROW WITH FOUR ROWS ALTOGETHER WHAT WOULD THE SURFACE MEASUREMENT BE

cues.text: The area is twenty-eight square metres. The perimeter is a different quantity: seven plus four plus seven plus four is twenty-two metres. Area counts the cover; perimeter measures the border.
cues.asr_text: THE AREA IS TWENTY EIGHT SQUARE METRES THE PERIMETER IS A DIFFERENT QUANTITY SEVEN PLUS FOUR PLUS SEVEN PLUS FOUR IS TWENTY TWO METRES AREA COUNTS THE COVER PARIMETER MEASURES THE BORDER

cues.text: Adding eight and five does not count the tiles covering an eight-by-five rectangle. It counts only two side lengths. To find area, use all five rows of eight equal squares, with no gaps or overlaps.
cues.chapter: Square units are not side lengths
cues.asr_text: ADDING EIGHT AND FIVE DOES NOT COUNT THE TILES COVERING IN EIGHT BY FIVE RECTANGLE IT COUNTS ONLY TWO SIDE LENGTHS TO FIND AREA USE ALL FIVE ROWS OF EIGHT EQUAL SQUARES WITH NO GAPS OR OVERLAPS

cues.text: A rectangle has six columns and four rows of unit squares. What is its area? Look at the model, and keep your prediction in mind.
cues.asr_text: A RECTANGLE HAS SIX COLUMNS AND FOUR ROWS OF UNIT SQUARES WHAT IS ITS AREA LOOK AT THE MODEL AND KEEP YOUR PREDICTION IN MIND

cues.text: Four groups of six make twenty-four square units. You can check by counting the tiles or adding six four times. No tile should be counted twice.
cues.asr_text: FOUR GROUPS OF SIX MAKE TWENTY FOUR SQUARE UNITS YOU CAN CHECK BY COUNTING THE TILES OR ADDING SIX FOUR TIMES NO TILE SHOULD BE COUNTED TWICE

cues.text: Area counts equal squares covering a surface. Use rows and columns to count efficiently and always label the square unit. Draw two rectangles with the same area on squared paper. Do they have to have the same perimeter? Explain with a drawing. Reflect on which model helped you and why. Now try the MathMagic practice, and explain your thinking to someone.
board: Cover with equal squares, without gaps.
Same area need not mean the same perimeter.
